body.p: The Office Action mailed February 24, 2023 (hereinafter "Office Action") has been carefully reviewed, and Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the rejections of Applicant's claims, particularly in view of the foregoing amendments and the remarks that follow.
Claims 1-13 were previously pending. By the present submission, claims 1, 10, and 13 have been amended, and claims 2 and 3 have been cancelled. No claims are newly added herein.
Claim 1 has been amended to incorporate the features of original claims 2 and 3, which are cancelled herein, wherein corresponding amendments have also been made to independent claims 10 and 13.

Claim 1 has also been amended to refer to the vehicle motion management system as being connectable to a motion support system coupled with at least one actuator configured to apply a torque to at least one wheel of the vehicle, and to provide that the vehicle motion management system is configured to "transmit a control signal indicative of the desired torque to the motion support system for use in controlling the at least one actuator to apply a torque to at least one wheel of the actuator."

The amendments to Applicant's claims are fully supported by and consistent with the originally-filed application. No new matter within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. § 132(a) and 37 C.F.R. § 1.121 has been introduced by the foregoing amendments.

p.u: Response to Rejection of Claims 1-9 under 35 U.S.C.

body.p: Claim 1-9 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as allegedly being "directed to an abstract idea," specifically "the abstract idea of determining signals based on the operating conditions of the vehicle, specifically the step of "transmit a control signal indicative of the desired torque and the wheel speed limit to the motion support system." (Office Action, page 6.) Applicant respectfully disagrees with the foregoing rejections, for at least the reasons set out below.

The framework for determining subject matter eligibility for patent claims is summarized in part in a flowchart appearing at MPEP 2103, as modified by the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (hereinafter, "2019 PEG"), wherein a composite flowchart incorporating the 2019 PEG is set out below.

The analysis under Step 2A Prong Two requires an Examiner to "evaluate integration into
a practical application by: (1) identifying whether there are any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually
and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application." (MPEP 21 06.04(d)(JI).) In particular:

[T]the way in which the additional elements use or interact with the exception may integrate it into a practical application. Accordingly, the additional limitations should not be evaluated in a vacuum, completely separate from the recited judicial exception. Instead, the analysis should take into consideration all the claim limitations and how those limitations interact and impact each other when
evaluating whether the exception is integrated into a practical application. (MPEP
2106.04(d)(III) (emphasis added).)

The point is echoed in MPEP 2106.05(I), which states that "[e]valuating additional elements to determine whether they amount to an inventive concept requires considering them both individually and in combination to ensure that they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception itself." Because this approach considers all claim elements, the Supreme Court has noted that "it is consistent with the general rule that patent claims 'must be considered as a whole."' Alice Corp., 573 U.S. at 218 n.3, 110 USPQ2d at 1981 (quoting Diamond v. Diehr, 450 U.S. 175, 188, 209 USPQ 1, 8-9 (1981)). Consideration of the elements in combination is particularly important, because even if an additional element does not amount to significantly more on its own, it can still amount to significantly more when considered in combination with the other elements of the claim. See, e.g., Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect, 827 F.3d 1042, 1051, 119 USPQ2d 1370, 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2016) (process reciting combination of individually well-known freezing and thawing steps was "far from routine and conventional" and thus eligible); BASCOM Global Internet Servs. v. AT&T Mobility LLC, 827 F.3d 1341, 1350, 119 USPQ2d 1236, 1242 (Fed. Cir. 2016) (inventive concept may be found in the non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of components that are individually well-known and conventional).

On page 6 of the Office Action, as part of applying Step 2A of the patentable subject matter framework, the Examiner asserted that claim 1 is directed to an abstract idea on the basis that "the claim merely recites generally performing the steps of the system and sending a signal without integrating them in the control of the system, or a further practical application." The same page of the Office Action noted that "[i]ndependent claims 10 & 13, while similar to claim 1, are not rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101, as the claims [10 & 13] disclose the control of torque on the vehicle, and not merely the mathematical computation of signal to send."

As noted previously herein, claim 1 has been amended to recite that the vehicle motion management system is configured (among other things) to "transmit a control signal indicative of the desired torque to the motion support system for use in controlling the at least one actuator to apply a torque to at least one wheel of the actuator." Accordingly, claim 1 has been amended to include limitations analogous to those recited in claims 10 and 13 concerning the control of an at least one actuator to apply a torque to at least one wheel of a vehicle

Thus, contrary to the conclusion reached at page 7 of the Office Action, amended claim 1 is not merely directed toward an abstract idea, amended claim 1 does recite additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application, and amended claim 1 does recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Accordingly, amended claim 1 and the claims depending therefrom are directed to patent-eligible subject matter and is not subject to further rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101.
For at least the foregoing reasons, withdrawal of all rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 is respectfully requested.

Applicant respectfully disagrees with the foregoing rejections in application to the claims as amended herein for at least the reasons set out below.

As discussed in MPEP § 2131, "[a] claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference." "The identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as is contained in the ... claim."2 Because the hallmark of anticipation is prior invention, the prior art reference - in order to anticipate under 35 U.S.C. § 102 - must not only disclose all elements of the claim within the four corners of the document, but must also disclose those elements "arranged as in the claim."3 An allegation that a prior art reference anticipates a patent claim cannot be based on sections of a reference taken in isolation; rather "the cited sections must be read in context."4 This is consistent with the pronouncement of the Federal Circuit that "[t]he well established rule of law is that each prior art reference must be evaluated as an entirety, and that all of the prior art must be evaluated as a whole."5

In order for an obviousness rejection to be appropriate, a prior art reference (or references when combined) must typically disclose all of the claim limitations.6 Additionally, "there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness" to establish obviousness.7
The Supreme Court has confirmed that references that teach away from the invention are evidence of the non-obviousness of a claimed invention, and reaffirmed the principle that a fact

In considering a reference for its effect on patentability, the reference is required to be considered in its entirety, including portions that teach away from the invention under consideration. Simply stated, the prior art must be considered as a whole."1 "It is impermissible within the framework of section 103 to pick and choose from any one reference only so much of it as will support a given position, to the exclusion of other parts necessary to the full appreciation of what such reference fairly suggests to one of ordinary skill in the art."12 The Federal Circuit and its predecessor court have repeatedly held that if references taken in combination would produce a "seemingly inoperative" device, then such references teach away from the combination and cannot serve as predicates for a primafacie case of obviousness.13

p.u: and Its Dependents over Ford and Suhre

body.p: As noted previously herein, claim 1 has been amended to include the limitations of original claims 2 and 3. Since claims 2 and 3 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as allegedly being obvious over Ford in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,542,806 to Suhre (hereinafter, "Suhre"), patentable distinctions of amended claim 1 over Ford in view of Suhre are provided below.

Ford disclose a traction control system for a vehicle having a first wheel driven by a first electric motor having a first set of coil windings and a first controller arranged to control current in the coil windings for generating a drive torque for driving the first wheel, and a second controller arranged to determine a maximum wheel velocity and a minimum wheel velocity. (Ford, Abstract.) The second controller communicates to the first controller the maximum and minimum values and a torque demand value. (Ford, Abstract.)

In connection with the rejection of claim 2, page 10 of the Office Action conceded that Ford does not disclose determining the speed limit based on the desired torque; however, the same page of the Office Action pointed to Suhre (e.g., Col. 8, lines 3-5 and Col. 3, lines 20-25 thereof) as disclosing the slip ratio being determined as function of tractive force command (received for the accelerator pedal of the driven vehicle), such that page 11 of the Office Action contended that one of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to combine Suhre with Ford in "order to include the motion request in the computation of speed limit and thereby yield outputs better suited to the specific motion request made by the driver of the vehicle."

In connection with the rejection of claim 3, page 11 of the Office Action pointed to paragraph [0061] of Ford as disclosing sending maximum and minimum speed limit values, as well as individual torque demand requests, to each motor. The same page of the Office Action

14 See Mintz v. Dietz & Watson, 679 F.3d 1372, 1379 (Fed. Cir. 2012) ("Simply because the technology can be easily understood does not mean that it will satisfy the legal standard of obviousness. In fact, objective consideration of simple technology is often the most difficult because, once the problem and solution appear together in the patent disclosure, the advance seems self-evident. Instead, the proper analysis requires a form of amnesia that 'forgets' the invention and analyzes the prior art and understanding of the problem at the date of invention.")
(Emphasis added.)

contended that "transmitting both the maximum and minimum speed limits to the motor instead of individually, along with the torque request, is recognized by one of ordinary skill in the art to not meaningfully affect operation of the system, as the maximum speed limit would not be operable when the torque is below zero (i.e., in a braking condition), and the minimum speed limit would not be operable when the torque is above zero (i.e., in an accelerating condition).

Applicant disagrees with the conclusion that it would have been obvious to one skilled in the art to have combined Ford and Suhre to arrive at the subject matter of amended claim 1, and further disagrees with the Examiner's contention that the subject matter of amended claim 1 (incorporating the features of prior claims 2 and 3) would not meaningfully affect system operation.

As disclosed by the present application, by using the vehicle motion management system, (i.e. the upper layer control module) to determine if an upper of lower speed limit should be transmitted to the motion support system (i.e. the lower layer control module), will substantially reduce the data bandwidth in the data sent between these modules.

Thus, sending only the upper limit or only or lower limit, will, contrary to the Examiner's opinion, meaningfully affect the operation of the system, as the response time will be even further reduced (and therefore improved).

Additionally, by letting the vehicle motion management system discriminate between a torque level above or below zero, and transmitting a specific wheel speed limit based on this determination, will beneficially enable a simplified motion support system to be employed. Conversely, in the system according to Ford (whether or not combined with Suhre), the control devices 400 at the wheels must be programmed to enable positive and negative torque to be distinguished, and the control devices 400 use different wheel speed limits based on this determination. Turning back to the present case, the vehicle motion management system of claim 1 is connectable to a motion support system that uses the wheel speed limit the motion support system is instructed to use, such that the motion support system does not need to make any active decisions.

Moreover, the control unit 102 according to Ford is not disclosed as being able to transmit different wheel speed limits based on a positive torque (i.e., torque above zero) or negative torque (i.e., torque below zero), according to the final two clauses of amended claim 1.

Thus, the solution described in Ford will exhibit a slower response (e.g., due to increased bandwidth requirements), require additional programming, and exhibit reduced functionality, in comparison to the vehicle motion management system (coupleable to a motion support system) the present invention.
For at least the foregoing reasons, the subject matter of amended claim 1 is patentably distinguished over the hypothetical combination of Ford and Suhre.
